significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish a form-(iii) law: the benefit of grammatical marking depends on the interaction between whether a category is obligatorily expressed and whether that exact category is task-relevant—the claimed "DOUBLE DISSOCIATION"—rather than merely showing that language and accuracy are associated. This would fix predictions across evidential/source tracking, number, definiteness, and gender tasks and establish both a targeted behavioral phenomenon and a causal forcing-function account, although "hard-wires attention" remains less determinate as an internal mechanism than the behavioral interaction itself. MGSM (Shi et al., ICLR 2023) documents large language-conditioned differences in multilingual reasoning, so settling this interaction would materially constrain whether such differences should be explained and addressed at the level of task-matched grammatical information; a null interaction would distinctly rule out obligatory marking as a general scaffold in current LLMs, though not other language effects. The topic-substitution check lowers no score: the generic topic "language and AI intelligence" would not supply this feature-by-task law or its double-dissociation prediction.

reach.justification: The concrete handles are the "marking*relevance interaction coefficient and effect size" and the intervention to "INSERT explicit marking (or STRIP it)," which together yield a prompt-design rule rather than only an explanation. The insertion rule is ex ante because task-relevant grammatical information can be added before reasoning, leaving an action window for prompt designers and multilingual-model practitioners. After language- or model-specific measurement, the conclusion predicts the sign and selectivity of the effect—benefit when the marked dimension matters and no general benefit otherwise—so what transfers is a relation, not merely a procedure for rediscovering an arbitrary direction; the asserted scope covers four grammatical dimensions and several multilingual model families, though not all tasks or architectures. The topic-substitution check passes: the broad language–intelligence topic alone provides neither this usable marking rule nor its targeted transfer prediction.
